label: Trajectory Generation
notes: This chapter, spanning printed pages 325 through 352, asks how geometric waypoints become a smooth, executable time history. We separate the path, which names where to go, from the trajectory, which names when to be there, and we keep both objects visible throughout the lecture.

label: Path versus Trajectory
notes: A path is a geometric trace parameterized by s running from zero to one; a trajectory attaches a clock through the time scaling s of t. The chain rule shows velocity and acceleration are products of path shape and clock derivatives, so timing is a genuine design decision, not an afterthought.

label: Polynomial Time Scaling
notes: Boundary conditions decide polynomial degree. A cubic has four coefficients, enough to pin both endpoints and zero the endpoint velocities, while a quintic adds two more coefficients so endpoint accelerations also vanish. The number of constraints you impose dictates how many free coefficients the scaling must carry.

label: Cubic Time Scaling
notes: The cubic time scaling produces a parabolic velocity profile peaking at the midpoint and a linear acceleration profile that jumps discontinuously at the endpoints. That nonzero starting acceleration demands an instantaneous torque step, which torque-limited actuators cannot deliver cleanly, motivating the smoother quintic alternative.

label: Quintic Time Scaling
notes: The quintic time scaling satisfies six boundary conditions: position, velocity, and acceleration at both ends. Its velocity rises and falls smoothly while acceleration starts and returns to zero, eliminating the torque jumps of the cubic. The notebook verifies the quintic endpoint acceleration norm falls below tolerance.

label: Velocity and Acceleration Profiles
notes: Comparing profiles makes the tradeoff concrete. The trapezoidal scaling reaches a top speed fastest and is time efficient, the cubic is smoother in position, and the quintic is smoothest in acceleration. The path is identical in every case, so all differences in demand come from the scalar clock alone.

label: Trapezoidal Velocity Profile
notes: A trapezoidal profile accelerates at a constant rate, coasts at a velocity limit, then decelerates symmetrically, making it the time-optimal scaling under separate velocity and acceleration bounds. Its acceleration is piecewise constant, so its jerk is unbounded at the corners, which the S-curve profile later rounds off.

label: Time Scaling Scales Demands
notes: Stretching a fixed quintic move over duration T scales peak speed like one over T and peak acceleration like one over T squared. The notebook confirms a four-to-one speed ratio and sixteen-to-one acceleration ratio across durations, explaining why simply slowing a motion down recovers feasibility.

label: Joint-Space versus Task-Space Paths
notes: A joint-space straight line interpolates joint vectors and is simple but bends in task space. A task-space straight line keeps the end-effector on a Cartesian line, which is intuitive for the operator but may pass through singularities or exceed joint limits. The representation you choose shapes feasibility.

label: Via Points and Interpolation
notes: Via points let a tool pass near inspection poses without stopping. Interpolating positions alone can hide velocity discontinuities at the knots, so a careful generator matches velocities and sometimes accelerations across segments. Smooth position is necessary but never sufficient for a torque-controlled machine.

label: Time-Optimal Phase Plane
notes: Time-optimal scaling along a fixed path becomes a feasibility problem in the s, s-dot phase plane. A maximum-velocity limit curve marks where any faster motion violates an actuator constraint. The optimal policy bangs between maximum acceleration and maximum braking while staying strictly below that limit curve.

label: Summary and Takeaways
notes: Trajectory generation cleanly separates geometry from timing. Boundary derivatives are design constraints that fix polynomial degree, time scaling rescales velocity and acceleration demands predictably, and the phase plane certifies that a timing respects actuator limits. These habits carry directly into the motion planning chapters that follow.
